CNMS Introduction – Object Types
▪ CNMS monitors two different types of objects:
- Hosts and Services
- Allows differentiation between network problems (host XYZ not reachable) and a problem on a host
(hardware or software problem)
▪ A Host is usually a physical device in the network (like a server, switch, router, …)
▪ Services are:
- Host resources (like disks, CPUs, fans, raid, …)
- A network service (http, smtp, …)
- A status of an application
▪ A host can have one or more services

Host

CNMS Introduction – Host States
▪ Ping (ICMP) is used to determine the host status:
- UP: The Host is up and running
- DOWN: The host is down, no ICMP replies were received from this host.
- UNREACHABLE: A network component, between CNMS and host, is down. Configuration of
network dependencies (or network topology) is needed.

Overview: Monitored Linux System Parameters
▪ The following parameters are monitored on each Linux system
- CPU Usage
• Average CPU usage in percent

• Memory consumption in percent

Overview: Monitored Linux System Parameters
▪ CPU usage
- Monitoring of average CPU usage in percent
- Output:
• Total CPU usage
• User CPU usage (CPU usage by processes
that doesn’t belong to the kernel)
• System (kernel) CPU usage
• Wait (or IO Wait), input and output
operations like writing to disk
- Critical and warning limits are configurable
and can be applied to either total, user,
system or wait CPU usage
- Default thresholds:
• Warning: 60% (total)
• Critical: 90% (total)

Overview: Monitored Linux System Parameters
▪ Memory
- The amount of the used memory is monitored
- “Real” memory (RAM) and Swap (disk space, which is used as memory)
- Warning limit: 90% memory used
- Critical: 95% memory used
▪ Free Disk Space
- Checks the used disk space on all partitions (except /boot)
- Warning: > 90% disk space used
- Critical: > 95% disk space used
- Default partitioning scheme:
/ Root-Partition
/var Partition for Logfiles, Caches, …
/boot Boot Partition (Kernel and Boot loader)

Overview: Monitored Linux System Parameters
▪ Time Synchronization
- Warning when the time deviation is larger than 0.2 sec.
- Critical: larger than 0.5 sec.
▪ Bonded Interfaces
- Bonding:
• Two physical network interfaces build one logical interface. One of these two physical interfaces is used
as a hot standby interface
- Warning status
• Is displayed, when one physical interface is not available
- Critical status
• Is displayed, when both physical interfaces are down or the bonded interface is down

CNMS Actions – Event Console
▪ The CNMS core component Nagios is using regular queries (polling) to determine various
component states (hard disk state, cpu usage, etc.)
▪ Events, like for example “user authentication error”, are not caught by simple polling.
▪ The CNMS “Event Console”:
- Receives messages or events from syslog service, snmp trap daemon, or other applications
- Processes and classifies incoming events with rules
- Rules are used to classify incoming messages, based on message attributes (syslog priority, trap
oid, trap content, syslog message content, etc.)
- Provides a current event status view in the CNMS GUI

CNMS Actions – Event Console
▪ Remote (or local) host sends event message either via
syslog or snmp trap
▪ Syslog messages are received by Rsyslog daemon
▪ Traps are
- Received by snmptrap daemon
- Passed to snmp trap translator (snmptt):
• Translates cryptic trap messages to something meaningful
• Add a severity to the trap (ok, warning, critical)
- traps are passed to Rsyslog daemon
▪ Rsyslog sends all syslog messages and traps to
mkeventd, the central process of the Event Console.
▪ Received events are accessible in the CNMS Web GUI

CNMS Actions – Event Console
▪ Supported Traps in CNMS
- Link Up / Link Down traps
- Traps from Comsoft applications
- Hardware health related traps from HP servers
- Various CISCO traps: BRIDGE-MIB, CISCO-IPSEC-MIB,
CISCO-SYSLOG-MIB, etc.
▪ Traps must be activated on the relevant component (e.g.
on the network switch or server)
